units.unit: Hong Kong should tighten rent control on subdivided units
Tenants in tiny subdivided flats are poor with little bargaining power, so landlords can raise rent easily
Housing is a basic need and bad conditions hurt health and children
The government can pair control with other help so landlords do not just leave
The 'other help stops landlords leaving' part is just a guess
Needs sources showing the strongest opposing view first, then ones testing the three reasons
D5 is the landlords' view, the strongest opposing side
D6 is an academic paper on supply that tests whether landlords leave
D5p3 says landlords have no real data on margins, so the exit threat is less credible
D6p1 and D6p3 hurt the view: hard caps shrink stock and the poor tenants lose units
Refined position: tighten via second-generation limits on increases within tenancies, not a hard cap on level
D6p2 says second-generation controls show small or null stock effects and the 2021 ordinance is one
That explains the stable stock in the D2 index, but that is only a claim about D2, which hasn't been read
The 2021 ordinance is already in place, so 'tighten' is unclear
Needs data and enforcement sources
Data first: it must show whether SDU stock and rents stayed stable after 2021 and whether the numbers are reliable
Then enforcement, to see whether existing rules actually work
D2 is the data on stock and rents after 2021, needed to check D6's claim
D11 gives tenants' own preferences, which tests the reason that tenants need protection
D2 supports D6: stock grew from 107,300 in 2021 to 111,200 in 2025 while the ordinance was in place
SDU rents grew slower than general rents
Rent burden still rose from 31 to 34 percent, so tenants are still squeezed
Post-2023 figures are extrapolated
D11 changes the idea: 61 percent of tenants would trade a rent rise for three-year security
'Tighten' should mean tenure security plus a light band on initial rents, not a hard cap
Did not expect tenants to prefer security over rent level
D11 is right that tenants value security and a hard cap is a bad tool
D11 is an NGO with a preferred policy, and the survey asks about a trade, which does not mean rent level does not matter
D2p2 shows rent burden worsened to 34 percent, so some rent control is still needed
Doubt enforcement can be spared, because the ordinance only works if landlords follow it
Enforcement source must show whether enforcement is currently weak, mainly inspection capacity and register completeness
D10 is about inspection capacity and the register, which is what was asked for, though it is a draft so treat it carefully
D9 tells whether a tighter design could be blocked or cost compensation
D10p1 says inspection covers under 6 percent of stock a year and a band needs a register taking 40 to 60 staff-years
D10p2 and D10p3 say the most exploited tenants, newest arrivals and those without written agreements, are the ones enforcement would miss
D9p1 says the 2021 style is legally safe but leaves initial rent unregulated
D9p2 says a published band is defensible but needs a survey system that does not exist
Position changes again: tighten in steps — build register and survey data first, add tenure security now, bring in an initial-rent band after
A tighter rule without enforcement would be a promise that helps the tenants who are already best off
Picks option 1, claim-evidence-objection-reply
Claim is staged tightening
Objections are the landlords' exit threat (D5, D6) and the NGO view that caps are the wrong tool (D11)
The reply uses D2, D9 and D10
D5 is the objection (landlords exit) but D6 is academic and used in the reply because it says the exit effect is small for the 2021 type of control
D11 is partly conceded: caps are the wrong tool, so the staged plan puts tenure security first
Answers the part saying rent does not matter using the burden rising to 34 percent
The source needs to show who is hurt most today, the newest arrivals and tenants without written agreements, because that carries the claim that enforcement must reach them first
D10p3 mentions D1 and D4
A study measuring who bears the harm would carry the claim best, with a first-hand account as colour
D1 should describe who the SDU tenants are and the 2021 ordinance
D4 is a first-hand account from a tenant without a written agreement, showing the harm D10 talks about
D1p1 and D1p2: SDU tenants pay a 15 to 25 percent per-square-foot premium and are mostly new arrivals, single parents and people waiting for public housing
That keeps the reason that they have little bargaining power
D1p3 says the 2021 ordinance did not cap the initial rent, so 'tighten' means the initial rent
D4p1: Mrs Wong, with no written agreement, says the ordinance changed nothing
She wants a hard cap but reports two flats turned into storage (D4p3), so her belief that landlords cannot exit is not safe
One person is anecdote, so use her as colour only
Keeps the staged position
D11 is half right
Queue length is the root problem (D1p2 says waits are about five and a half years)
Agrees inspection of fire and ventilation matters
The staged plan builds the register first, which also helps inspections
D2p2 and D4p1 show rent still hurts
Rent control alone is not enough, so tenure security comes with it
Accepts that if the register cannot be built, a band should wait
The reply answers the inspection-cost point
Concedes the queue-length point: rent control cannot fix the queue, so public housing speed is the real long-term answer and the plan is a stopgap while people wait
Main weakness is that D10 is a draft marked not for circulation and D10p3 says part was to be struck from the public version
Will cite D10 but say what it is
